title.narrative: Centre for Human Rights - University of Pretoria
Centre for Human Rights - University of Pretoria

description.narrative: Centre för mänskliga rättigheter (centret) vid juridiska fakulteten vid Pretorias universitet arbetar för att främja implementeringen av mänskliga rättigheter i Afrika genom kapacitetsuppbyggnad, opinionsbildning, strategisk litigering och forskning. Centret, som grundades 1986, har investerat i att bygga ett nätverk av människorättsförsvarare över hela kontinenten genom sina akademiska program och alumninätverk. De har etablerat sig som en respekterade partner till organen i det afrikanska människorättssystemet till vilka de tillhandahåller juridisk expertis. De tillhandahåller även tekniskt stöd till stater att till exempel rapportera mot internationella fördrag, inte minst Maputoprotokollet. Centret är en ny partner till Sida och kontaktades efter att Sida konsulterat nyckelaktörer inom den regionala människorättsarkitekturen samt givare som pekat på centrets betydelse inom detta område. Programmet och programmålen Programmet Strengthening the Protection of Sexual and Reproductive Health Rights in Africa har det övergripande målet att stärka skyddet av sexuella och reproduktiva rättigheter i Afrika genom att: 1) påverka tolkningen av juridisk normer kring SRHR, kvinnors rättigheter och flickors rättigheter på regional (Afrika) och nationell nivå 2) främja ansvarsutkrävande kring implementering av kring juridiska normer för SRHR i den afrikanska regionen. 3) stärka produktion och förvaltning av kunskap om sexuella och reproduktiva rättigheter i Afrika 4) harmonisera regionala, juridiska normer för sexuella och reproduktiva rättigheter Programmet syftar till att stötta regionala mekanismer för mänskliga rättigheter såväl som statliga aktörer för att uppfylla sina skyldigheter. Det är Sidas bedömning att centret, en expertorganisation inom området mänskliga rättigheter, tydligt har identifierat vilka mänskliga rättigheter man vill stärka och vilka makthavare (duty bearers) de ska rikta sig till. Centret syftar också till att öka medvetenheten bland rättighetsbärare – inklusive kvinnorättsorganisationer och hbtqi+-organisationer – om åtaganden som är relevanta för dem, samt stötta dem att ställa makthavare till svars. Innovation och kunskapsförvaltning är både en gränsöverskridande prioritet för centret och ett explicit program-mål. Eftersom centret både är en forskningsinstitution och civilsamhällesaktör har de goda förutsättningar att använda resultaten av sin forskning i sitt påverkans- och kapacitetsstärkande arbete för att skapa förändring. Genom sitt välrenommerade masterprogram, med alumner välplacerade både nationellt och regionalt, har de också ett brett nätverk för att sprida sina kunskapsprodukter i och en medveten plan för att göra det. Den huvudsakliga målgruppen för detta programmet är kvinnor, inklusive äldre kvinnor, flickor och hbtqi+-personer i Afrika. För att uppnå förbättrad SRHR för dessa grupper riktar centret sig mot statliga organ (inklusive oberoende statliga institutioner som nationella människorättsinstitut, NHRIs), för att förbättra deras kapacitet att leverera, följa upp nationella åtaganden för att skydda dessa rättigheter. Programmet riktar sig också till mottagarna själva för att förbättra deras ansvarsutkrävande förmåga i förhållande till dessa rättigheter.

Sweden's Strategy for SRHR in Africa (2022-2026) is expected to contribute to increased respect for and enjoyment of SRHR for all, where one of the priorities include strengthened capacity and political will for African human rights bodies as well as AU member states to domesticate, implement and report on priority commitments, including the Maputo Protocol. The strategy also aims to increase accountability for SRHR, where both the state and civils society play an important role in for example ensuring that regional commitments are implemented and reported on.Over the recent past, we have seen progress in above areas. An increasing number of legal norms and standards related to sexuality and reproduction are adopted or interpreted progressively and in parts of the continent we see a strong demand for accountability for the implementation of commitments related to gender and SRHR. These progressive developments are however undercut by resistance to the generous interpretation and application of SRHR legal norms at national and regional levels and by limited capacity for monitoring and accountability. As a result, the exercise of SRHR continues to be characterised by poor health outcomes and rights violations, including the exclusion of marginalised populations from access to SRHR services.Against this background, and as a result of the conclusions drawn in the MDPA and in the operationalisation of the new strategy, Sweden's regional team for SRHR decided to expand its engagement with the regional human rights architecture. As such, the scoping found that there was a need to prioritize on which regional frameworks and commitments to focus on, namely on the Maputo Protocol. It also found that the regional human rights mechanisms needs support in connecting the region and country level to advance SRHR and contribute to a stronger African human rights architecture.The team approached the Centre for Human Rights after consulting key actors within the regional human right's architecture as well as donors who indicated the importance of the Centre in this field. The Centre works to enhance implementation of human rights norms in Africa through capacity building, advocacy, litigation and research. The Centre has invested in building a community of human rights advocates across the continent through its academic programmes and alumni network and has established itself as a partner to the institutions of the African human rights system providing legal expertise, as well as technical support to states in reporting to international treaties, notably the Maputo protocol.After a series of meetings with the Centre, they submitted a proposal titled Strengthening the Protection of Sexual and Reproductive Health Rights in Africa. The overarching goal for the proposed project is to improve protection of gender and SRHR norms in Africa by:1) influencing the interpretation of SRHR, women’s rights norms, and the rights of the girl-child at the regional (Africa) and national levels2) fostering accountability for SRHR norm implementation in the African region3) strengthen sexual and reproductive rights knowledge generation and management in Africa4) harmonise regional norms on sexual and reproductive rights

The overall goal of the program is to strengthen the protection of sexual and reproductive rights in Africa. The goal will be achieved through four objectives:
1. To influence the interpretation of SRHR, women's rights norms and the rights of the girl-child at the regional and national levels.
2. To foster accountability for SRHR norm implementation in the Africa region.
3. To strengthen SRR knowledge generation and management in Africa
4. To promote the harmonization of African regional norms in sexual reproductive rights

Center for Human Rights, CHR, and Sida entered into agreement in January, 2023 hence there is limited results reporting at this time.
For the achievement of the overall objectives of the project the Center's organization is set up in following units:
The units for Sexual and Reproductive Rights in Africa (SRRA) and Human Rights and Democratization in Africa (HRDA) offer two academic programs focusing on SRHR within an African context. There are also a number of students registered for LLD/PhD/DPhil in these fields.
The Women's Rights Unit (WRU) is engaged in advocacy to ensure the Africa-wide ratification of the Maputo Protocol. The unit provides technical support to strengthen the capacity of government officials and state parties to prepare and submit their periodic reports under the Maputo Protocol, and it further supports the work of the Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Women in Africa.
The Children's Rights Unit (CRU) works through research, capacity strengthening, advocacy and training, to contribute to the discourse on the rights of children in Africa. It aims to influence laws, policies, and practice at national and regional levels, and it collaborates with the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child.
The Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression, and Sex Characteristics Unit (SOGIESC) advocates for and works towards equality, inclusion, non-discrimination, non-violence, and non-heterosexism for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, intersex, queer, questioning, and asexual persons (LGBTIQ persons). Its work is done through advocacy, training, policy development, social action, as well as providing legal aid for LGBTIQ victims of discrimination and violence.
The Litigation and Implementation Unit (LIU) has the mandate to engage in human rights litigation and asses the implementation of decisions of international and regional human rights bodies. Its aim is to strategically use the law through the instrumentality of judicial and quasi-judicial institutions to enforce human rights, prevent violation of human rights and or seek redress for human rights violations.
During 2023 the Center undertook a number of courses and workshops, gathering key stakeholders from all over the continent to enhance their understanding of sexual and reproductive rights and opportunities of women, linked to the human rights architecture in Africa, such as the African Charter and Maputo Protocol. By building the knowledge on the existing legal frameworks for advocating for SRHR and creating platforms for effective cross-learning on strategies for the advancement of these rights, the diverse pool of participants are capacitated to adequately engage with the issues on SRHR at the national and regional level in their specific areas of work or advocacy.
For instance, a validation workshop (CHR and Sierra Leone MFA) on Sierra Leone's State Report on the African Charter and Maputo Protocol enabled the submission of the report to the African Commission, which in turn makes it possible for the Commission to exercise its protection mandate in ensuring state compliance with its treaty obligations and hold Sierra Leone accountable for the implementation of the rights in the treaties.
In order to influence norms that promote SRHR in the region, courses were held on SOGIE issues, LGBTIQ activism and Resolution 275. This increases the number of LGBTIQ advocates across the continent capacitated to influence those norms. The Center also held a conference aiming to bring together commissioners from Human Rights Institutions and Commissions from across the continent in order to disseminate information on Resolution 275 and to facilitate capacity building on how Resolution 275 may be utilized by the institutions.
A research colloquium was also planned on digital rights and innovations related to sexual reproductive rights in Africa. Papers presented at the colloquium will culminated in the first series of publications on SRHR under the Sida support. This is aimed at strengthening SRHR knowledge generation and management in Africa.
The Center held a training on strategic litigation of SRHR claims before national and regional mechanisms expected to increase the quality and quantity of cases on the continent, which will improve accountability and implementation of SRHR norms in Africa. One immediate outcome was that some ongoing and potential SRHR claims were identified and CHR has commenced on engagements with relevant actors to provide support for the potential and ongoing cases.
Furthermore, the Center provides overall technical support to the AU by sending interns/researchers to each of the Human Rights Bodies. They also support the AU Commission and Committee on ad hoc basis on various aspects of SRHR and gender issues through research studies, development of normative documents such as general comments, organizing and participating in related panels during sessions.
In addition to their own project activities, the Center has been helpful in sharing their expertise with Sida in terms of the human rights architecture in Africa(in a seminar for embassy and HQ staff) as well as the composition and operations of the opposition(during the partner meeting in Pretoria).
